Figure 1.RealMe creates immersive volumetric video from sparse and low-quality captures.When directly optimized from sparse observations, FTGS(Wang et al., 2025e)struggles to maintain consistent reconstruction quality (left).
In contrast, RealMe generates 2K multi-view videos with high visual quality and strong 4D consistency (middle), which further supports high-quality volumetric video reconstruction (right).Teaser comparison. The left part shows FTGS reconstruction from sparse observations. The middle part shows RealMe generation with 2K visual quality and 4D consistency. The right part shows RealMe reconstruction as volumetric video.

Figure 2.Overview of our framework.Given sparse and low-quality captures, RealMe first initializes a coarse 4DGS(Wang et al., 2025e)representation and uses it to render novel-view videos; in parallel, we detect ROIs with an offline detector(Guo and Deng, 2024)and crop the input captures to preserve local detail cues.
These auxiliary videos are fed into a high-resolution video diffusion model to produce enhanced videos, which are then used together with the input captures to optimize the 4DGS representation for volumetric video reconstruction.
The detailed model architecture is illustrated inFig.3.Overview of the RealMe framework, from limited input captures through auxiliary data construction and video enhancement to 4D reconstruction.

Figure 3.Model architecture.We use a ControlNet(Zhang et al., 2023)branch to inject control signals from condition latents and text features.
DiT blocks use these signals with layout-aware positional embeddings to denoise noisy latents via factorized spatio-temporal attention.A diagram of the video diffusion model architecture.

Figure 5.Qualitative comparison for novel view synthesis onRealVV.Given the same sparse input captures, RealMe produces higher visual quality and more consistent novel views than optimization-based and generation-based baselines.
Diffuman4D(Jin et al., 2025)cannot generate scene backgrounds and generalizes poorly to zoomed-in long-focus views, while RealMe preserves both human appearance and surrounding scene content.Qualitative comparison for novel view synthesis on RealVV.

Figure 6.Qualitative comparison for detail enhancement onRealVV.Starting from low-resolution inputs, STAR(Xie et al., 2025)and FlashVSR(Zhuang et al., 2025)tend to produce over-smoothed regions or artificial local textures.
In contrast, RealMe restores richer facial details, hair structures, and clothing textures with a more natural appearance.
Pleasezoom into better inspect the local visual quality.Qualitative comparison for detail enhancement on RealVV.

Figure 7.Additional qualitative comparisons for novel view synthesis onRealVV.We compare FTGS(Wang et al., 2025e), DIFIX3D+(Wu et al., 2025b), Diffuman4D(Jin et al., 2025), RealMe, and the ground truth under the same sparse-capture setting.
The examples cover both short-focus and long-focus views.
RealMe better preserves scene backgrounds, human appearance, and view-dependent details.Additional qualitative comparisons for novel view synthesis on RealVV.

Figure 8.Additional qualitative comparisons for novel view synthesis on DNA-Rendering.We compare FTGS(Wang et al., 2025e), DIFIX3D+(Wu et al., 2025b), Diffuman4D(Jin et al., 2025), RealMe, and the ground truth using eight input views.
The top and bottom four rows show two evaluation sequences across different held-out viewpoints and timestamps.Additional qualitative comparisons for novel view synthesis on DNA-Rendering.

Figure 9.Additional qualitative comparisons on long-focus views.We compare FTGS(Wang et al., 2025e), DIFIX3D+(Wu et al., 2025b), generated views from RealMe, 4D reconstruction from RealMe, and the ground truth.
Long-focus views stress the ability to recover high-resolution appearance under limited input coverage.
RealMe produces cleaner details and more faithful scene appearance in these zoomed-in views.Additional qualitative comparisons on long-focus views.

Figure 10.Qualitative ablation on latent frequency loss.We compare generated RGB results with and without latent frequency loss (LFL), the RGB error map, and the corresponding low-frequency and high-frequency latent visualizations.
The latent maps show that LFL better preserves high-frequency structures such as silhouettes, facial details, and clothing boundaries, complementing the quantitative ablation in the main paper.Qualitative ablation on latent frequency loss.

Figure 11.RealVV dataset overview.We show representative samples fromRealVV, including short-focus captures, long-focus captures, foreground masks, and camera-rig views across different scenes.RealVV dataset overview with representative short-focus captures, long-focus captures, foreground masks, and camera-rig views.
